params.text:
Welcome to the Module

This module — part of the BriGRETE (Bridging the Gap in Research Ethics Training & Education) Erasmus+ project — equips clinical researchers, students, and healthcare professionals with the knowledge to navigate the ethical and legal landscape created by artificial intelligence in clinical research.

By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • Acknowledge the core concepts of ethics and law in research;
  • Identify key normative documents governing AI in clinical settings;
  • Recognise the practical consequences of using AI in scientific protocols and data analysis;
  • Analyse the ethical and legal limits designed to protect human dignity and fundamental rights.

metadata.title: Learning Objectives – four core competency steps on a DNA helix

params.text: This module is designed for: Researchers (early-, mid-, and senior-career) and the broader research community; Research Ethics Committee (REC) members; Teachers and students; and other healthcare professionals and the general public.

Step 1: Acknowledge concepts of ethics and law in the research field.
Step 2: Identify relevant past and present normative documents on ethics in clinical research.
Step 3: Realise the practical relevance of AI devices in scientific protocols and data analysis.
Step 4: Analyse the limits established by ethical and legal regimes to protect human dignity and rights.
Approximately 60–75 minutes, including interactive knowledge checks and the final assessment.

params.alt: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence – Turing 1950, McCarthy & Hayes 1969, and the three types of AI intelligence

metadata.title: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence – Turing 1950, McCarthy & Hayes 1969, and the three types of AI intelligence

params.text:
The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence has developed from early theoretical investigations — Alan Turing's landmark 1950 paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence and John McCarthy and Patrick Hayes's 1969 paper Some Philosophical Problems from the Standpoint of Artificial Intelligence, an early investigation of the philosophical and logical foundations of AI — into systems of rapidly growing sophistication, driven by the proliferation of information technology and telematics.

John McCarthy introduced the term ‘artificial intelligence’ in the 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence; the workshop took place in 1956. Today the field encompasses learning machines with capabilities in language processing, vision, speech, planning, and robotics.

Today, AI systems improve three interdependent types of intelligence in clinical contexts:
Processes visual and auditory data — for example, analysing medical imaging, interpreting diagnostic scans, and transcribing patient records from speech.
Handles natural language processing and knowledge representation — enabling AI to read scientific literature, generate clinical summaries, and model disease relationships.
Covers planning, robotics, and actionable clinical intelligence — supporting treatment recommendations, surgical robots, and adaptive trial protocols.

params.title: Review key facts about AI's origins.

params.alt: Transforming Clinical Paradigms – three fields of AI influence: Investigational Development, Practical Implementation, Communication and Dissemination

metadata.title: Transforming Clinical Paradigms – three fields of AI influence: Investigational Development, Practical Implementation, Communication and Dissemination

params.text:
Three Fields of AI Influence

AI transforms clinical research across three interconnected fields:

AI enables new laboratory experiments and scientific techniques, more efficient rationalization methods for data analysis, and advanced storage and treatment of research data — allowing scientists to develop new biological models, drug candidates, and treatment pathways at unprecedented speed.

AI endorses new methodologies for research design and management, the execution of clinical trials, and the automated generation of diagnostic reports — optimising protocol writing, patient selection, and real-time monitoring to increase study precision.

AI promotes scientific discourse through wider communication networks between researchers and provides faster mechanisms for sharing knowledge, accelerating peer review and public reporting of findings.

params.alt: AI Clinical Research Applications – Stage 1: Investigational Development, Stage 2: Trial Conduct, Stage 3: Data Treatment

metadata.title: AI Clinical Research Applications – Stage 1: Investigational Development, Stage 2: Trial Conduct, Stage 3: Data Treatment

params.text:
The Three Stages of the Research Pipeline

Looking at the research process as a pipeline, AI integrates at every stage:

  • Stage 1 – Investigational Development: AI allows the development of new models, drugs, and treatments by processing biological data at scale.
  • Stage 2 – Trial Conduct: AI enhances protocol writing, data analysis, patient selection, and monitoring procedures during active trials.
  • Stage 3 – Data Treatment: AI manages the settlement, treatment, and communication of personal and research data after the trial concludes.

Stage 3 is particularly sensitive from an ethical perspective: it is the moment when personal identity is converted into raw, manipulable research data.

params.title: Review the fields and stages.

dialogs.text: What does AI enable in Stage 1 – Investigational Development?
dialogs.answer: Development of new biological models, drugs, and treatments; new laboratory experiments; efficient data rationalization.

dialogs.text: What does AI enhance in Stage 2 – Trial Conduct?
dialogs.answer: Protocol writing, patient selection, data analysis, and real-time monitoring during clinical trials.

dialogs.text: What does Stage 3 – Data Treatment involve?
dialogs.answer: Settlement, processing, and communication of personal and research data; the most sensitive stage for governance.

dialogs.text: Which AI influence field promotes faster knowledge sharing between researchers?
dialogs.answer: Communication and Dissemination.

params.alt: Navigating the Risks of AI Integration – main challenges mapped to ethical and legal principles

metadata.title: Navigating the Risks of AI Integration – main challenges mapped to ethical and legal principles

params.text:
Main Challenges in AI-Integrated Clinical Research

The integration of AI into clinical research introduces five interrelated challenges that researchers and ethics committees must actively manage:
AI systems process sensitive biometric and health data. Without rigorous controls, this data can be accessed, misused, or leaked — violating the participant's fundamental right to privacy.
AI-generated outputs can be manipulated, falsified, or biased by flawed training data, undermining the scientific validity of the study.
Ensuring that the information and data used in AI models is genuine and verifiable is a primary challenge for research safety.
Research data — especially when processed through cloud-based AI platforms — is vulnerable to breaches, ransomware, and unauthorised access.
Both trial participants and the research team face physical, psychological, and legal risks when AI systems produce incorrect or biased conclusions.

params.alt: Core Ethical and Legal Principles – four pillars supporting research integrity: Human Dignity, Privacy Protection, Equality and Non-Discrimination, Security

metadata.title: Core Ethical and Legal Principles – four pillars supporting research integrity: Human Dignity, Privacy Protection, Equality and Non-Discrimination, Security

params.text:
Four Core Ethical & Legal Principles

These challenges are addressed by four foundational principles that together uphold research integrity:

  1. Human Dignity: Every research participant must be treated as an end in themselves, never merely as a source of data.
  2. Privacy Protection: Personal and health data must be collected, stored, and used within strict legal boundaries.
  3. Equality & Non-Discrimination: AI systems must not perpetuate cultural, racial, economic, or gender biases. A DEI (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion) framework is essential.
  4. Security: Research data and the systems that process it must be protected against threats at every stage of the lifecycle.

params.alt: Advantages and Disadvantages of AI in Clinical Research – opportunities and risks

metadata.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of AI in Clinical Research – opportunities and risks

params.text:
Advantages and Disadvantages of AI in Clinical Research

Advantages (Opportunities)

  • A powerful tool for rapid clinical research development.
  • An instrument for scientific and medical innovation.
  • Significant time-saving capabilities across the research pipeline.
  • A means to provide easier, broader access to health care globally.

Disadvantages (Risks)

  • Complexities and vulnerabilities in data protection.
  • Cultural, economic, racial, and gender biases built into algorithms through unrepresentative training data.
  • The danger of moving from human substitution (using AI as an instrumental tool) to human replacement in society — raising profound ethical questions about the role of human judgment.

params.alt: Health as a Fundamental Human Right – UDHR Article 25/1 and alignment with UN SDGs

metadata.title: Health as a Fundamental Human Right – UDHR Article 25/1 and alignment with UN SDGs

params.text:
Health as a Fundamental Human Right

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 25/1, 1948) establishes that everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of themselves and their family. This right is directly linked to the purpose of clinical research.

The WHO Constitution (1946) defines health not merely as the absence of disease or infirmity, but as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being.

Alignment with the UN 2030 SDGs

Clinical research contributes directly to four Sustainable Development Goals:

  • SDG 3: Good health and well-being
  • SDG 9: Industry, innovation, and infrastructure
  • SDG 10: Reduced inequalities
  • SDG 16: Peace, justice, and strong institutions

params.alt: Dimensions of Human Rights – Scope (Universalist/Relativist), Intentionality (Procedural/Normative), Construction (Formal-liberal/Critical-material)

metadata.title: Dimensions of Human Rights – Scope (Universalist/Relativist), Intentionality (Procedural/Normative), Construction (Formal-liberal/Critical-material)

params.text:
Three Dimensions of Human Rights

Human rights scholarship analyses rights across three analytical dimensions:

Universalist perspectives argue that human rights apply equally to all human beings regardless of cultural context.
Relativist perspectives hold that rights are shaped by cultural, social, and historical contexts.

Procedural (adjective) perspectives focus on the processes and methods through which rights are implemented and enforced.
Normative (substantive) perspectives focus on the material content and outcomes that rights are intended to achieve.

Formal-liberal perspectives emphasise legal frameworks and institutional processes.
Critical-material perspectives focus on structural inequalities and social conditions that rights must address.

params.alt: Evolution of Human Rights Generations – 1st to 5th Generation timeline

metadata.title: Evolution of Human Rights Generations – 1st to 5th Generation timeline

params.text:
The Five Generations of Human Rights

Human rights have evolved in successive generations, each responding to new social and technological challenges:
Focus on freedom: civil liberties, life, human dignity, and political participation. Rooted in the values of the French Revolution (liberté).
Focus on equality: rights to work, social protection, housing, and education. Emerged from socialist and labour movements.
Focus on solidarity: collective rights including development, environment, and peace. Reflect post-colonial and global justice concerns.
Focus on identity in the digital and genetic age: Internet access, virtual reality, genetic rights, and protection from technoscientific threats. Most directly relevant to AI in clinical research.
Focus on democracy and good governance in highly automated and interconnected societies.

params.alt: The 4th Generation Identity Quadrant – Subjective Identity, Objective Identity, Species Identity, Historical Continuity

metadata.title: The 4th Generation Identity Quadrant – Subjective Identity, Objective Identity, Species Identity, Historical Continuity

params.text:
4th Generation Identity Rights

The fourth generation introduces four distinct identity rights particularly relevant to AI-driven research:
The right that technoscience does not make us doubt our internal sense of self. Protects against neurotechnologies that might alter one's self-perception.
The right not to lose our sense of reality — for example, protection against deep fakes and AI-generated disinformation that blurs truth.
The right to clarity on whether entities are biological or non-biological — protecting against confusion between humans, AI systems, chimeras, or synthetic products.
The right to a recognisable world, avoiding a dystopian singularity or absolute rupture with our cultural and social past.

dialogs.text: Which generation of HR covers genetics and digital identity?

dialogs.answer: Dystopian singularity — an absolute rupture with our cultural past caused by disruptive technologies.

dialogs.text: What value underpins the Fifth Generation of Human Rights?
dialogs.answer: Sociability — democracy and good governance in highly automated societies.

metadata.title: Ethics, Law, and Governance in Clinical Research
metadata.extraTitle: Ethics, Law, and Governance in Clinical Research

params.alt: Decisive Ethical Issues in AI Clinical Research – Human-centric, Data-centric, and System-centric nodes

metadata.title: Decisive Ethical Issues in AI Clinical Research – Human-centric, Data-centric, and System-centric nodes

params.text:
Decisive Ethical Issues in AI Clinical Research

Ethical governance of AI in clinical research operates across three interconnected clusters of concern:

Beneficence & Respect: AI must be used in ways that benefit participants and uphold their dignity.
Consent: Rigorous informed consent is a non-negotiable prerequisite for all AI-mediated research on persons.
Trust: Participants and society must be able to trust that AI systems are used responsibly.

Confidentiality & Privacy: Research data — especially biometric and health data — must be protected from unauthorised access.
Data Protection & Governance: Legal frameworks (particularly the GDPR) must be applied rigorously to the entire data lifecycle.

Transparency & Explainability: Researchers must be able to understand and account for how an AI system reaches its conclusions.
Scientific/Medical Leges Artis (Standards of Practice): AI systems must operate within established professional and scientific standards.
Accountability & Continuous Monitoring: Systems must be auditable and monitored throughout the research process.

params.alt: Ethics vs. Legal Regulation – Ethics is reflective, Law is mandatory

metadata.title: Ethics vs. Legal Regulation – Ethics is reflective, Law is mandatory

params.text:
Ethics vs. Legal Regulation

Clinical research is governed by two complementary but distinct pillars:

Ethics (Reflective)Law (Mandatory)Points out substantially and formally reflective practicesEstablishes substantially and formally mandatory principlesGuides actions according to cultural values and professional principlesSets strict rules, prohibitions, and procedures for the legality of clinical researchAssesses validity, reliability, and legitimacy of researchProtects human life and fundamental rights by force of the state

These two forces meet in the Research Ethics Committee (REC) — the mandatory institutional body that translates reflective ethical principles into legal authorisations.

params.alt: Valid, Reliable, Legitimate – ethics in health research must be constantly updated and reassessed

metadata.title: Valid, Reliable, Legitimate – ethics in health research must be constantly updated and reassessed

params.text:
Valid, Reliable, Legitimate

"In health research, ethics involves a set of principles and norms that must be constantly updated and reassessed to ensure that it is valid, reliable, legitimate, and representative."

— Gomes Lima Junior et al.

Because AI evolves rapidly, ethical norms must be dynamic — not static. Every research project utilising AI must demonstrate these four qualities.

params.alt: Ethical Data Treatment Imperatives – five-spoke wheel: Personal & Team Relationships, Collection, Storage & Privacy, Informed Consent, Management of Research Results, Transparency & Objectivity

metadata.title: Ethical Data Treatment Imperatives – five-spoke wheel: Personal & Team Relationships, Collection, Storage & Privacy, Informed Consent, Management of Research Results, Transparency & Objectivity

params.text:
Five Ethical Data Treatment Imperatives

The treatment of personal and research data must follow five unavoidable procedural requirements:
Navigating the personal dynamics and responsibilities within the research team, ensuring clear roles and ethical accountability.
Ensuring strict adherence to GDPR and research ethics standards for data collection, ownership, storage, and protection across the entire data lifecycle.
Obtaining rigorous, specific, and freely-given informed consent from each participant — covering exactly what their data will be used for.
Ensuring secure, ethical handling of research data and results, including appropriate archiving and disposal.
Ensuring complete transparency in every single step of the research process, from design to publication.

dialogs.answer: The ability to understand and account for how an AI system reaches its conclusions.

dialogs.text: What is the role of 'leges artis' in clinical research?
dialogs.answer: It refers to the professional and scientific standards of practice — the mandatory rules for scientific conduct.

dialogs.text: In Hegel's distinction, what does 'Sittlichkeit' refer to?

dialogs.answer: Law is characterised by hetero-determination, tertiality, comparability, and attributive bilaterality.

dialogs.answer: Paul Max Fritz Jahr.

params.alt: The Global Normative Framework – timeline from UDHR 1948 to EU Charter 2000

metadata.title: The Global Normative Framework – timeline from UDHR 1948 to EU Charter 2000

params.text:
The Global Normative Framework

Clinical research is regulated by a layered international legal architecture built over seven decades. Key milestones include:

Article 25 establishes the right to an adequate standard of living including health and medical care. Article 12 prohibits arbitrary interference with privacy — foundational for data protection in research.
The first binding European human rights treaty. Article 8 protects the right to private life, directly relevant to clinical data.

The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Article 6/1) protects the inherent right to life. The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (Article 12) recognises the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health.
The World Medical Association's foundational ethical principles for medical research involving human participants — first drafted in 1964 and regularly updated.

panels.title: 1997 – Oviedo Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine

params.text: The Council of Europe convention specifically protecting human beings regarding the application of biology and medicine. Focuses on consent, comparable effectiveness, and protection of research participants.

panels.title: 2000 – Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union

params.text: Legally binding in the EU since 2009 (Lisbon Treaty), this Charter codifies rights to human dignity (Article 1), privacy (Article 7), and data protection (Article 8).

params.alt: The Oviedo Convention Boundaries – three mandatory conditions for research on humans

metadata.title: The Oviedo Convention Boundaries – three mandatory conditions for research on humans

params.text:
The Oviedo Convention: Three Mandatory Conditions

Under Article 16 of the Oviedo Convention, research on a person may only be undertaken if three cumulative conditions are met:

  1. No Alternative: There is no alternative of comparable effectiveness to research on humans — all other research avenues must first be exhausted.
  2. Proportionate Risk: The risks incurred by the participant are not disproportionate to the potential research benefits.
  3. Independent Approval: The project is approved by a competent, multidisciplinary ethics committee after independent examination.

Additionally, informed consent may be freely withdrawn at any time by the participant (Article 16/v).

params.alt: EU Clinical Trials Regulation – prior authorization, scientific and ethical review by ethics committee

metadata.title: EU Clinical Trials Regulation – prior authorization, scientific and ethical review by ethics committee

params.text:
EU Clinical Trials Regulation

The EU Clinical Trials Regulation requires that every clinical trial:

  • Undergoes rigorous scientific and ethical review;
  • Receives prior authorisation before commencement;
  • Has its ethical review performed by an ethics committee under Member State law.

This regulation directly addresses trials that use AI platforms — any new use of an AI system within a trial constitutes a distinct action requiring fresh authorisation.

params.alt: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR 2016/679) – core mandate and clinical relevance

metadata.title: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR 2016/679) – core mandate and clinical relevance

params.text:
GDPR – General Data Protection Regulation (2016/679)

Core Mandate: The GDPR protects natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and the free movement of such data.

Clinical Relevance: The GDPR forms the baseline legal requirement for how clinical research data — especially the biometric and health data required to feed AI models — must be securely handled, consented to, and anonymised within the European regulatory framework.

Key provisions for clinical AI research:

  • Article 17 – Right to Erasure ('Right to be Forgotten'): Participants may request deletion of their personal data.
  • Article 22 – Automated Decision-Making: Individuals have the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects.
  • Special categories of data (health and biometric data) require explicit consent and enhanced protection.

params.alt: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act – three core purposes: promote human-centric AI, ensure protection, protect against harmful effects

metadata.title: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act – three core purposes: promote human-centric AI, ensure protection, protect against harmful effects

params.alt: EU AI Act: Scope (Article 2), Context, and Goal – balancing risk analysis with technological innovation

metadata.title: EU AI Act: Scope (Article 2), Context, and Goal – balancing risk analysis with technological innovation

params.text:
The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689)

The EU AI Act — while not exclusively designed for healthcare — has profound implications for clinical research AI systems.

Core Purposes

  1. Promote human-centric, trustworthy AI.
  2. Ensure a high level of protection for health, safety, and fundamental rights.
  3. Protect against harmful effects of AI systems within the Union.

Scope (Article 2)

The Act applies to providers placing AI systems on the EU market regardless of where those providers are established — including providers from third countries. AI systems developed solely for scientific R&D are exempted (Article 2/6).

AI System Definition (Article 3)

An AI system is defined as a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, capable of inferring outputs such as predictions or decisions from received inputs.

params.alt: Prohibited AI Practices (Article 5) – Subliminal Manipulation and Biometric Categorization

metadata.title: Prohibited AI Practices (Article 5) – Subliminal Manipulation and Biometric Categorization

params.alt: Prohibited AI Practices (Article 5) – Subliminal Manipulation and Exploitation of Vulnerabilities

metadata.title: Prohibited AI Practices (Article 5) – Subliminal Manipulation and Exploitation of Vulnerabilities

params.text:
Prohibited AI Practices (Article 5)

Article 5 of the EU AI Act establishes an absolute prohibition on certain AI practices:

Prohibited: placing on the market or using AI systems that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness to materially distort their behaviour, impairing informed decisions and causing significant harm.
Prohibited: exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability, or socioeconomic situation to distort behaviour in a way that causes harm — directly relevant to vulnerable clinical trial participants.

Prohibited: AI systems that categorise natural persons based on biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation.

params.alt: High-Risk AI Systems and Human Oversight – conditions for exemption and the absolute mandate on profiling

metadata.title: High-Risk AI Systems and Human Oversight – conditions for exemption and the absolute mandate on profiling

params.text:
High-Risk AI Systems & Human Oversight

Most AI systems used in clinical research are classified as high-risk. A system is NOT considered high-risk only if it:

  • Performs a narrow procedural task;
  • Improves the result of a previously completed human activity;
  • Detects decision-making patterns but does not replace human assessment or review;
  • Performs a preparatory task for an assessment.

The Absolute Mandate: If an AI system performs profiling of natural persons, it is always considered high-risk — regardless of the above. Providers must document assessments and register systems with national competent authorities.

params.alt: The Unified AI Compliance Framework – pyramid: Ethics base, Human Rights middle, Legal top, Protected Clinical Trial Participant pinnacle

metadata.title: The Unified AI Compliance Framework – pyramid: Ethics base, Human Rights middle, Legal top, Protected Clinical Trial Participant pinnacle

params.text:
The Unified AI Compliance Framework

Compliant AI-integrated clinical research requires a layered framework with the protected clinical trial participant at its pinnacle:

  • Base Layer – Ethics: Continuous reflection, Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) as foundational values.
  • Middle Layer – Human Rights: Protection of 4th Generation subjective and objective identity rights.
  • Top Layer – Legal Parameters: AI Act prohibitions and Oviedo Convention risk ratios as binding legal limits.
  • Pinnacle: The protected clinical trial participant — the ultimate purpose of the entire framework.

params.alt: Case Study: AI Platforms & Consent – Background, Conflict, and Stakeholders

metadata.title: Case Study: AI Platforms & Consent – Background, Conflict, and Stakeholders

params.text:
The Scenario

Background & Action

A PhD student researcher conducts a non-interventional clinical trial on a patient with a degenerative disease. The patient gave informed consent to participate. The project and informed consent document received a favourable decision from the competent ethics committee.

The study involved inputting the patient's personal and clinical data into an AI development platform to discover new treatment advantages.

The Conflict

After the study ended, the researcher decided to use the collected data for a different study using the same AI platform — without obtaining new consent from the patient.

Stakeholders

  • PhD Student Researcher
  • Vulnerable Patient
  • Competent Ethics Committee

params.alt: Case Study Ethical Resolution – Can the data be repurposed without intervention? Two resolutions.

metadata.title: Case Study Ethical Resolution – Can the data be repurposed without intervention? Two resolutions.

params.text:
The Ethical Resolution

Core Question: Can the data be repurposed without a new intervention?

The Ethics Committee's Verdict: No.

Resolution 1 – Strict Boundaries of Consent

Personal data and informed consent must be strictly obtained, reserved, and used only for the specific objectives referenced in the original research project. Data collected for Trial A cannot be used for Trial B without fresh consent.

Resolution 2 – AI Platform Implications

The creation or utilisation of an AI platform for a completely different purpose constitutes a distinct and new use of personal and clinical data. Therefore, the researcher must:

  1. Design a brand new research project;
  2. Obtain a specific, renewed informed consent document directly from the patient.

This case illustrates how the GDPR's data minimisation principle, the Oviedo Convention's consent requirements, and the EU Clinical Trials Regulation's prior authorisation requirement all converge to protect the participant.

params.question: In this case study, why could the researcher NOT reuse the patient's data for a new AI study?

answers.text: Because personal data must be used only for the specific objectives stated in the original consent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Informed consent is strictly scoped — it covers only the specific research purpose consented to.

answers.text: Because the AI platform was no longer available after the trial

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The AI platform was still available — the issue is about consent scope, not platform access.

answers.text: Because the ethics committee had lost jurisdiction after the study ended

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ethics committees retain authority; jurisdiction does not expire with the study.

answers.text: Because GDPR prohibits all AI use in clinical research

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GDPR regulates AI use; it does not prohibit it. The issue here is consent scope.

params.text:
Module Summary

You have completed Ethics and Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Research. Here are the key takeaways:

On Artificial Intelligence

  • AI integrates into clinical research across three stages (investigational development, trial conduct, data treatment) and three fields of influence (perceptual, cognitive, decision-making intelligence).
  • AI brings significant advantages — speed, innovation, access — but also real risks: data protection vulnerabilities, algorithmic biases, and the danger of replacing human judgment.

On Human Rights

  • Health is a fundamental human right (UDHR Article 25), and clinical research is directly aligned with SDG 3.
  • We now operate in the 4th Generation of Human Rights — the era of technoscience — where digital and genetic identity require the same protection as the physical body.

On Ethics and Law

  • Ethics is reflective; law is mandatory. Both are essential, and the REC bridges them.
  • Ethical norms must be constantly updated to remain valid, reliable, legitimate, and representative.
  • Five data treatment imperatives apply to every AI-mediated study: relationships, data lifecycle, consent, management, and objectivity.

On the Legal Framework

  • The international normative framework spans from the UDHR (1948) to the EU AI Act (2024).
  • The Oviedo Convention's three mandatory conditions, the GDPR's data protection requirements, and the EU AI Act's risk classification together form the legal backbone of ethical clinical AI research.
  • The case study demonstrates that new AI use = new consent — always.

"The integrity of 21st-century medicine depends on the balance between computational power and the rigorous protection of the individuals who provide its data."

Key Legal Instruments

  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UN, 1948). un.org
  • International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (UN, 1966). ohchr.org
  • International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (UN, 1966). ohchr.org
  • WMA Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964, revised 2013). wma.net
  • Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine (Oviedo Convention) (Council of Europe, 1997). coe.int
  • Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (EU, 2000/2009). europarl.europa.eu
  • General Data Protection Regulation – GDPR (Regulation 2016/679). gdpr-info.eu
  • EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689). artificialintelligenceact.eu
  • EU Clinical Trials Regulation (No 536/2014). eur-lex.europa.eu

Key Texts

  • Domingos, P. (2015). The Master Algorithm. Basic Books.
  • Turing, A. (1950). Computing Machinery and Intelligence. Mind, 59(236), 433–460.
  • McCarthy, J., Minsky, M. L., Rochester, N., & Shannon, C. E. (1955). A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence.
  • McCarthy, J., & Hayes, P. J. (1969). Some Philosophical Problems from the Standpoint of Artificial Intelligence. In B. Meltzer & D. Michie (Eds.), Machine Intelligence 4 (pp. 463–502). Edinburgh University Press.
  • Gomes Lima Junior, et al. Ethics in health research and the use of AI in radiology (cited in module).
  • WHO Constitution (1946). Preamble definition of health.
  • Jahr, P. (1927). Bio-Ethik: eine Umschau über die ethischen Beziehungen des Menschen zu Tier und Pflanze. Kosmos.
